newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-BALTIC MARKETS NEED BIGGER, MORE OPEN COMPANIES.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BALTIC MARKETS NEED BIGGER, MORE OPEN COMPANIES.

text.p: The emerging markets of the Baltc states can mushroom and speed the transition to a market economy but bigger companies, more transparency and aggressive marketing are needed, foreign investors said on Thursday.
They were speaking at a two-day conference on the Baltic capital markets, which began in the Swedish capital Wednesday.
It brought together senior government officials, central bankers, bourse officials, investors, brokers and analysts.

"The Baltics just don't have enough companies in terms of numbers or companies that are liquid right now," said Hamid Ladjevardi, a portfolio manager with one of the leading investment funds in the Baltics, the U.S.-based Baltic Fund.
"There just is not enough...dissemination of timely information," noting that one promising sign was the banking sector, which has taken the lead in being more open.
"More liquid stock markets will have broader benefits...liquidity and transparency give creditors more confidence," he said.
The Baltic bourses have pinned their hopes on the privatisation of large enterprises to boost liquidity.
Uldis Cerps, president of the Riga bourse, told the conference the capitalisation of his market was expected to grow to $1.6 billion from $300 million in the next 12 to 16 months.
New additions to the bourse will include the big Balta insurance company and Latvia's Savings Bank, he said.
But for now, the markets are seen as puny by many.

Dominic Pearce, head of securities research for Creditanstalt Investment Bank, noted that market capitalisation of the three Baltic states was $2.7 billion, compared to $36 billion for CEFTA states and $90 billion in Russia.
As a percentage of GDP, Estonia's market cap topped the regional list at 22.7 percent, Lithuania was 18.3 percent, and Latvia's stood at a mere five percent.
In contrast, the Czech Republic's market capitalisation was over 32 percent of its GDP.
"The Baltics are extremely small markets...they must be cleverer (than big markets) when it comes to presenting themselves," Pearce said.
He said that the Baltics had some strengths they could draw on when publicising themselves.
"The Baltics are natural transit economies between the nothern CIS and the West," he said.
He added that investors in the region were reassured by a commitment to control inflation and tough currency pegs, which were not found in the rest of eastern Europe.
Lithuania and Estonia both peg their currencies through a currency board system to the dollar and mark respectively while Latvia's currency is pegged to the IMF's SDR.
